items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1972-05-27
items.q: But Claude Kennedy was part of his clan... Now the fella that really brought some blues to Texas was a trumpet player from here... Lee Collins. That was another great technician.

ctx.x: I wondered because, you see, some guys I listen to, and I'm not mixing in any names, or any names, or any names. Well, the whole areas of the country, you didn't hear good blues from them. Whereas I hear Texas had good blues, you know. And you go back and you hear early New Orleans guys, to me they sounded like good blues players.

It was a different type of blues in Texas. You had, I can't recall the name of all of these players, you would have to come back to them. But Claude Kennedy was part of his clan, but he didn't lay on the blues. Now the fella that really brought some blues to Texas was a trumpet player from here, that died not so long ago in Chicago, maybe quite a few years ago, Lee Collins. That was another great technician. And Guy Kelly, which was no relation to Chris, those fellas had, they had some dreams, I'd say. A man has…
Well, your records, Troy Floyd, they're nice blues, you know, and then the little brutes. The blues singers, they're nice blues. Yeah.

items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1961-05-11
items.q: And another great trumpet player was playing around there. He's dead now. Lee Collins.

ctx.x: He's been following you around, huh?

He was one of the masters. So I said, yeah, I can play something else. So I started out and I tried to improvise one of the three I was playing. He says, that's the same one you've been playing all the time. But in volume it all, huh? He says, that's the same one. Right on the truck then. Yeah, that's right. Well, I left Mardi Gras with three pieces. I left there with the banjo, Richard McCarthy, and Lucian Johnson. And my first stop was Dallas, Texas. And I played at a honky-tonk in Dallas, Texas. It was on the…
Oh, yes. I knew him. Very much in Chicago.
